subtitle: Drawn from that night's Nightly Discourse Report: every political, cultural, and religious story, each put to a table of historical thinkers.

briefing.question: What is the first duty of a new majority: holding power to account, or governing for the people's immediate needs?
briefing.agreed: Oversight is a real duty, weighed against voters' priorities and held to a shared standard.
briefing.split: Madison, ambition checks ambition; Mill, watching is the job; Burke, repair not conquest; Washington, beware revenge.

briefing.question: When a complex system fails, is the fault in the people running it or in the system we have neglected to renew?
briefing.agreed: The failure implicates both system and people; look at design, upkeep and decisions.
briefing.split: Perrow, coupling makes it normal; Hamilton, name who decided; Aristotle, blame by foresight; Burke, shared debt.

briefing.question: Who should decide when a nation goes to war: the deliberative many or the decisive one?
briefing.agreed: Commanders need room, but a sustained war needs recognized authority and review.
briefing.split: Hamilton, command not declaration; Madison, Congress decides; Locke, prudence as trust; Aquinas, cause and intent.

briefing.question: Is a nation a single people whose majority should rule directly, or a union of communities whose voices must be balanced?
briefing.agreed: The people should choose; how votes are counted shapes whose voices matter.
briefing.split: Madison, amend openly; Hamilton, states may choose; Tocqueville, weaker barriers; Mill, equal votes and minorities.

briefing.question: Where does satire end and contempt begin, and should the same rule apply to everyone?
briefing.agreed: A roast may sting without penalty; judge the target, one rule for every group.
briefing.split: Aristotle, tact not buffoonery; Aristophanes, mock the powerful; Hobbes, laughter as superiority; Mill, one standard.

briefing.question: Should government stay neutral among a people's many heritages, or help celebrate them as a shared civic good?
briefing.agreed: Shared celebrations matter, and a law touching them should be clear.
briefing.split: Tocqueville, associations carry on; Rawls, access not removal; Fuller, fix the vagueness; Durkheim, rites bind if shared.

briefing.question: Do artists owe their audience what it expects, or is art free to change those expectations?
briefing.agreed: Art may change expectations but answers for its quality; buyers judge too.
briefing.split: Plato, what play forms; Aristotle, not for the crowd; Wilde, craft only; Eliot, earn a place; Hirschman, exit and voice.

briefing.question: Is a joke judged by its intent, its effect, or the moment it is told?
briefing.agreed: Intent matters, but a joke on a grave subject answers for its effect; no law.
briefing.split: Bergson, detachment fails; Aquinas, grave matter; Mill, consequences; Kant, persons never mere means.

briefing.question: What binds a public servant: shared civic symbols or personal conscience?
briefing.agreed: The oath binds through the promise to the Constitution; no religious test.
briefing.split: Locke, swear by conscience; Jefferson, scripture irrelevant to office; Hobbes, the book adds nothing; Rousseau, shared civic faith.

briefing.question: Can someone hold their faith as exclusively true and still govern all citizens as equals?
briefing.agreed: Exclusive faith and equal citizenship fit, if office never prejudices anyone.
briefing.split: Augustine, love every neighbor; Locke, law is civil; Williams, the office is civil; Rawls, public reasons.

briefing.question: Does Christ's kingship call Christians to rule a nation, or to witness within it?
briefing.agreed: Christians may shape public life; racial ranking contradicts the faith.
briefing.split: Augustine, a city of all nations; Leo XIII, honor without force; Douglass, impartial Christ; King, witness and justice.

sittings.headline: One router, ten thousand cancellations: who answers for Friday's nationwide ground stop?
sittings.question: When a complex system fails, is the fault in the people running it or in the system we have neglected to renew?

setup.text: The Transportation Secretary said Saturday that a router installed during a contractor's copper-to-fiber upgrade at a remote FAA site flooded the air-traffic network, triggering a roughly five-hour nationwide ground stop that cancelled nearly 10,000 flights; officials found no sign of a cyberattack and are still determining whether it was installer error or a faulty router. The Secretary blamed decades-old legacy equipment, the FAA chief called for $50 billion in upgrades, and House Democrats promised an oversight inquiry.

turn.text: I placed good humor in a mean between two faults. On one side, “they who exceed in the ridiculous are judged to be Buffoons and Vulgar, catching at it in any and every way and at any cost, and aiming rather at raising laughter than at saying what is seemly and at avoiding to pain the object of their wit.” (Nicomachean Ethics IV.x) On the other, “They, on the other hand, who would not for the world make a joke themselves and are displeased with such as do are thought to be Clownish and Stern.” (Nicomachean Ethics IV.x) So I do not side with those who say no joke should sting. A roast is a recognized occasion for teasing, and a man who cannot laugh at anything is himself at fault.

turn.text: Aristotle wants tact; I wanted the audience to squirm. I mocked the most powerful men in Athens by name, to their faces, in the theater. My hero tells the crowd: “Comedy too can sometimes discern what is right. A comedy that spares the powerful is a flattery, not a comedy.

I defined it without sentiment: “Sudden glory, is the passion which maketh those Grimaces called LAUGHTER; and is caused either by some sudden act of their own, that pleaseth them; or by the apprehension of some deformed thing in another, by comparison whereof they suddenly applaud themselves.” (Leviathan, Part I, ch. VI) We laugh, much of the time, because we feel suddenly above someone. That is why ridicule wounds and why crowds enjoy it.

sittings.question: Should government stay neutral among a people's many heritages, or help celebrate them as a shared civic good?

setup.text: Delray Beach says it will stop organizing, funding or promoting its long-running St. Patrick's Day parade and its Pride festival starting in 2027, citing a new state law that bars local governments from supporting events tied to ethnicity, sexual orientation or gender identity. The governor called the move malicious compliance and said the law does not require it; private groups may still run the events.

Leo XIII follows because the report names integralism and the Christendom tradition, citing his Immortale Dei, which gives the strongest papal case that a state owes public worship to God. Frederick Douglass is seated because his Narrative draws the sharpest line in American letters between a Christianity used to justify racial domination and the Christianity of Christ. Martin Luther King Jr. closes because the report names his Letter from Birmingham Jail on the image of God and universal dignity; he is in copyright and is paraphrased. John 18:36, Galatians 3:28 and Genesis 1:27, which the report names, are read by the moderator. The pastor, the speakers and the critics named in the report are context only.
